Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 1, verse 1 (part 1 of 2):

It is Meccan. It has also been said it is both Meccan and Medinan, since it was revealed once in Mecca and again in Medina. It is called Umm al-Qur'an (the Mother of the Qur'an) because it includes the meanings found in the Qur'an: praise of God Most High as He deserves, devotion through commands and prohibitions, and promise and warning. It is also called Surat al-Kanz (the Treasure) and al-Wafiyah (the Sufficient) for this reason. It is called Surat al-Hamd (the Chapter of Praise) and al-Mathani (the Oft-Repeated), because it is repeated in every rak'ah. It is called Surat al-Salat (the Chapter of Prayer), because prayer is virtuous or valid by reciting it in it. It is called Surat al-Shifa' (the Chapter of Healing) and al-Shafiyah. It has seven verses by agreement, except that some counted "the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favour" but not the basmalah, and some held the opposite view.

The reciters and jurists of Medina, Basra and Syria hold that the basmalah is not a verse of al-Fatihah or of any other surah. It was written only as a separator and for blessing by beginning with it, just as one begins with its mention in every matter of importance. This is the view of Abu Hanifa, may God have mercy on him, and those who followed him, and for this reason they do not recite it aloud in prayer. The reciters and jurists of Mecca and Kufa hold that it is a verse of al-Fatihah and of every surah, and al-Shafi'i and his companions, may God have mercy on them, held this view, and for this reason they recite it aloud. They said:

The early generation recorded it in the codex while enjoining that the Qur'an be kept pure, and for this reason they did not record "Amin." So if it were not from the Qur'an, they would not have recorded it. And from Ibn 'Abbas: "Whoever leaves it has left one hundred and fourteen verses of the Book of God Most High." [[A mawquf report, not known to be from him. What al-Bayhaqi has in al-Shu'ab from him is: "Whoever leaves bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim has left a verse of the Book of God." Ibn al-Hajib criticised what al-Zamakhshari reported, saying: "The correct figure is one hundred and thirteen," and al-Shahrazuri in al-Misbah mentioned it with this wording, adding that the reason it is not "one hundred and fourteen" is that Bara'a has no basmalah, end. Al-Bayhaqi in al-Shu'ab narrated from Ahmad ibn Hanbal that he said: "Whoever does not say bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim with every surah has left one hundred and thirteen verses of the Book of God Most High." I say: I have identified the source of the error in what al-Zamakhshari transmitted. Al-Hakim narrated in the biography of 'Abd Allah ibn al-Mubarak, with a chain of his own, from 'Ali al-Qashani, who said: "I saw 'Abd Allah ibn al-Mubarak raise his hands at the first takbir over the funeral, and at the second he lowered them slightly, and the prayers are like that." 'Ali said that 'Abd Allah said: "Whoever leaves bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim at the openings of surahs has left one hundred and thirteen verses." 'Abd Allah said: Hanzala ibn 'Abd Allah informed us from Shahr ibn Hawshab from Ibn 'Abbas, may God be pleased with him, who said: "Whoever leaves bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim has left a verse of the Book of God Most High." Since Ibn 'Abbas did not restrict it to a particular surah, Ibn al-Mubarak took it to apply to all, except Bara'a, so it came to one hundred and thirteen.]]

If you say: with what is the ba' connected? I say: with a omitted verb whose estimate is: "In the name of God I recite or I recite." [[Mahmud, may God have mercy on him, said: "The ba' in the basmalah is connected to an omitted verb whose estimate is: 'In the name of God I recite or I recite.'" Ahmad, may God have mercy on him, said: What the grammarians estimate is "I begin," and this is preferred for several reasons. First: the verb of beginning can be estimated in every basmalah one begins with, for any action other than the act of reading. The general, whose estimation is valid, is more fitting to be estimated. Do you not see that they estimate the complement of a prepositional phrase functioning as predicate, attribute, relative clause or circumstantial with "being/settling" wherever it occurs, and prefer it for the generality of its valid estimation? Second: the estimation of the verb of beginning is directly suited to the purpose of the basmalah, since its purpose is to be the starting point, so estimating the verb of beginning fits the position better. When you estimate "I recite," you mean "I begin the recitation," and what occurs in the course of recitation is also a recitation, but the basmalah is not prescribed except at the beginning. Among the proofs is the appearance of the verb of beginning in God's words: ﴿Recite in the name of your Lord﴾. The Prophet, peace be upon him, said: "Every important matter that is not begun with the name of God is cut off." This is not contradicted by what he mentioned about the appearance of the verb of reading in God's words ﴿Recite in the name of your Lord﴾, for the verb of reading appeared there because the more important matter is the reading, without regard to beginning it. Do you not see that the verb precedes its complement there because it is the more important? This is not so in the basmalah, for the estimated verb, whatever it is, is estimated after it, and if it were estimated before the name, the purpose of intending the beginning would be lost, since that is the more important in the basmalah. So it must be estimated. The discussion of this point will come.]] because whoever recites the basmalah is the one being recited, just as when a traveller alights or sets out and says "In the name of God and blessings," the meaning is: "In the name of God I alight," and "In the name of God I depart." Likewise the slaughterer, and every doer who begins his act with "In the name of God," is implying that the basmalah is what makes it a beginning. A parallel to omitting the complement of the preposition is God's words: ﴿To Pharaoh and his people with nine signs﴾, meaning: go with nine signs. Likewise the Arabs' supplication to the newly married: "With felicity and children," and the Bedouin's saying: "With prosperity and blessing," meaning: "you have married" or "you have wed." From this is the poet's line:

﻿

If you ask: why did you estimate the omitted element as coming later? I say: because if you began with the verb in the estimate, the noun would not be what one begins with, and the purpose of blessing by the name of God Most High at the start of your speech would be lost. As for the claim that fronting indicates exclusivity, there is a point to be examined, which will come, God willing.

I say: because the more important of the verb and its complement is the complement, since they used to begin with the names of their idols, saying "In the name of al-Lat, in the name of al-'Uzza," so the monotheist must intend the meaning of restricting the beginning to the name of God Most High, and this is done by fronting the noun and postponing the verb, as He did in His words ﴿You alone we worship﴾, where He explicitly fronted the noun to indicate restriction. The evidence for this is His words: ﴿In the name of God is its sailing and its anchoring﴾. If you say: but He said ﴿Recite in the name of your Lord﴾, fronting the verb? I say: there, fronting the verb was more effective, because it was the first surah revealed, so the command to read was more important.

If you ask: what is the meaning of the name of God being connected to the reading? [[Mahmud said: "If you ask what is the meaning of the name of God Most High being connected to the reading..." Ahmad, may God have mercy on him, said: His statement "the name of God is what makes its act deemed valid in law" deviates from the truth held by the People of the Sunna in two principles: first, that the name is the named; second, that the servant's act exists by God's power alone. On this basis, seeking help by the name of God means the servant acknowledges at the start of his act that it proceeds through his hands and that he is merely its locus, but its existence comes from God Most High, that is, by His power, submitting to God at the start of every act. Al-Zamakhshari, may God have mercy on him, cannot reach this verification, because he follows his desire in opposing the two principles mentioned, so he believes that the name of God Most High, which is the naming, is what gives legal validity to the act and not its existence, since its existence by his claim is by the servant's power. On this he built his statement. I say: his claim that according to the People of the Sunna the name is other than the named is disputed, and its verification has been discussed in other books.]] I say: there are two possibilities. The first is that it is connected to it as the pen is connected to the writing in your saying "I wrote with the pen," meaning that the believer, when he believes that his act will not be considered valid in law or accord with the Sunna unless it begins with mention of God's name, following His words, peace and blessings be upon him: "Every important matter that is not begun with the name of God is cut off" [[I have not seen it in this form. The well-known hadith is that of Abu Hurayra, through Qurra from al-Zuhri from Abu Salama from Abu Hurayra, may God be pleased with him, with the wording "Every matter not begun with praise of God is cut off," narrated by Abu 'Awana in his Sahih and the authors of the Sunan. Ahmad has from this route: "Not begun with mention of God is cut off or cut short." Al-Khatib in al-Jami' has, through Mubashshir ibn Isma'il from al-Zuhri, the wording "Not begun with bismillah al-Rahman al-Rahim is cut off," and its narrator from Mubashshir is unknown.]], any act becomes an act whose doing is attributed to the name of God, just as the writer does writing with the pen.

The second is that it is connected to it as the oil is connected to the growing in His words ﴿a tree growing with oil﴾ [[His statement "connected as oil to growing" suits the reading "tebnutu" from the causative of anbata, as will come. (A)]], meaning: seeking blessing by the name of God, I recite. Likewise the supplication to the newly married: "With felicity and children" means: "you have married accompanied by felicity and children." This second possibility is more eloquent and better. If you ask: how then does God Most High say "seeking blessing by the name of God, I recite"? I say: this is spoken on the tongues of servants, as a man recites poetry on another's tongue. Likewise ﴿Praise belongs to God, Lord of the worlds﴾ to its end, and much of the Qur'an follows this method. Its meaning is to teach His servants how to seek blessing by His name, and how to praise Him, glorify Him and exalt Him.

If you ask: letters of meaning that came in one letter should be built on the fatha, which is the sister of the sukun, such as the kaf of comparison, the lam of beginning, the waw and fa' of conjunction, and others; so why were the lam of possession and the ba' built on the kasra? I say: as for the lam, it is to distinguish it from the lam of beginning. As for the ba', it is because it is necessarily tied to being a particle and to the genitive. The word ism (name) is one of the ten nouns whose initial letters they built on the sukun, so when they pronounce it at the beginning they add a hamza, lest their beginning be with a sukun, since their habit is to begin with a moving sound and pause on a sukun, to keep their language free of every awkwardness and harshness, and because it is placed in a state of great firmness and solidity. When it occurs in the middle of speech, it needs no addition. Some did not add it and dispensed with it by moving the sukun, saying "sm" and "sm." He said:

"In the name of Him who in every surah is His mark."

It is one of the nouns whose final part is elided, like kid and dam. Its original form is sumw, as shown by its inflection: asma', sumwa, sumayt. Its derivation is from al-sumuww (height), because naming is an elevation of the named and an exalting of mention of him. From this the nickname is called nabz, from nabr, meaning raising the voice. Nabz is also the upper bark of the palm tree.

If you ask: why is the alif omitted in the script but written in "bism rabbika"? I say: in omitting it they followed the rule of connected speech rather than the beginning, on which the writing was founded, because of its frequent use. They said: the ba' was lengthened as compensation for dropping the alif. Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz said to his scribe: "Lengthen the ba', make the teeth show, and round the mim." The word Allah originally is al-Ilah. He said:

"God forbid that she be like a gazelle,
nor a statue, nor a noble heifer of wild cattle.
Rather she has added to all beauty
perfection, and fragrance upon every fragrance."

This is by al-Ba'ith ibn Hurayth about his beloved Umm al-Silsabil. It is said 'aadha, 'iyadh, mu'adh and 'awdh, meaning he sought refuge in another. So al-mu'adh is a verbal noun standing in for the verb. The dumya is an idol, or a figure of ivory or the like engraved with jewels. The 'aqila of everything is its most noble. The rabrab is a herd of wild cattle. He compared his beloved to a gazelle, a statue, and a noble heifer in his own mind, then found her better than these, so he retracted and sought God's refuge from that, as if he had sinned; or the meaning is: I do not liken her to these, though poets do. He used the emphatic la before what precedes it, which has the sense of negation: she is not like a gazelle, nor a statue, nor a noble heifer, but she has added perfection to all known beauty, or she has added to sensory beauty a spiritual perfection, and added from fragrance beyond every fragrance.]]

Its parallel: al-nas (people), originally al-unas. He said:

"Indeed the fates come upon
the unsuspecting people."

[[He likened the fates to people searching for one who deserves death, by way of metaphor, and "they come upon" is imaginative representation. The meaning: fates come upon people unawares and confound them so they cannot repel them. Al-unas is a collective noun without a singular of its own, derived from al-iynas, meaning sight because of its clarity, or from al-uns, the opposite of loneliness. The "unsuspecting" are those heedless of the coming of death, so it is a metonymy by way of the sending of the cause.]]

So the hamza is omitted and the definite article is substituted for it, which is why in address they say "Ya Allah" with a cut, as one says "Ya Ilah." The ilah, a noun of kind like man and horse, is a name applied to every worshipped being, whether by truth or falsehood, then it became predominant for the one worshipped in truth, just as najm is a name for every star and then became predominant for the Pleiades, and similarly sana for the year of drought, bayt for the Ka'ba, and kitab for Sibawayh's book. As for Allah without the hamza, it is specific to the one worshipped in truth and is not applied to any other. From this name are derived ta'alluh, ta'alluh and istiʼlah, as was said: istanwaqa and istahjara, in derivation from camel (naqa) and stone (hajar). If you ask: is it a noun or an adjective? I say: rather it is a noun, not an adjective, for you describe it but are not described by it; you do not say "a thing ilah," just as you do not say "a thing rajul." You say "ilah wahid samad," as you say "rajul karim khayr." Moreover, His attributes necessarily require a subject to which they apply, so if you made all of them adjectives they would not apply to a named subject, and that is impossible. If you ask: does this name have a derivation? I say: the meaning of derivation is that two or more forms share one meaning. The form of this name and the form of their saying "ʼalaha" (he was bewildered) share it, and from its siblings "dalaha" and "ʼalaha," which contain the meaning of bewilderment and astonishment. This is because the imaginations are bewildered in knowing the worshipped and the intelligent are astounded, and for this reason error multiplied, falsehood spread, and sound reflection became rare. If you ask: is its lam emphasized? I say: yes, al-Zajjaj mentioned that emphasizing it is the sunna, and all the Arabs follow it, and their unanimity on it is evidence that they inherited it from elder to elder.

Al-Rahman is on the pattern fa'lan from rahima, like ghadban and sakran from ghadiba and sakira; likewise al-Rahim is fa'il from it, like marid and saqim from marida and saqima. Al-Rahman has an intensity (mubalagha) that al-Rahim does not have. [[Mahmud said: "Al-Rahman has an intensity that al-Rahim does not have... etc." Ahmad, may God have mercy on him, said: The inference is not complete from the shortness or length of a form to the deficiency or completeness of intensity. Do you not see that some intensive patterns, such as fa'al in one of the forms, are shorter than fa'il, which has no intensity at all? As for their saying "Rahman of this world and the next" and "Rahim of this world," there is also no indication in it that rahman is more intense than rahim, for its upshot is that mercy from Him is by indicating its completeness. Do you not see that since darib is more general than darrab, darrab is more intense than it because of its specificity? So from the specificity of rahim it does not necessarily follow that it is less intense than rahman because of its generality.]] For this reason they said "Rahman of this world and the next" and "Rahim of this world," and they say that the increase in the form is for an increase in meaning.

Al-Zajjaj said regarding ghadban: it is one who is filled with anger. Among the Arabs' choice expressions that has lodged in my ear is that they call one of their mounts "al-shaqdaf," a light conveyance, not heavy like the Iraqi litters. On the road to Ta'if I said to one of them: "What is the name of this litter?" I meant the Iraqi litter. He said: "Is its name not al-shaqdaf?" I said: "Yes." He said: "This is its name, al-shaqndaf," so he increased the form of the name for an increase in what it names. It is among the dominant (ghalaba) attributes, like al-Dabaran, al-Ayyuq, and al-Sa'q, which is not used for anyone other than God, the Mighty and Majestic, just as "Allah" is among the dominant names. As for the Banu Hanifa's saying about Musaylima, "Rahman of Yamama," and the words of their poet about him:

"You are the rain of creation; may you never cease to be Rahman."

[[You have risen by glory, O son of the most noble ancestors... and you are the rain of creation, may you never cease to be Rahman. This is said by a man of the Banu Hanifa praising Musaylima the liar. He means: you have ascended by means of glory, O son of the most noble, on the paternal side; it is not meant specifically, but the origin in general. Had it been meant specifically, it would indicate blame. "Al-akramin" is a specifier (tamyiz), or "samawat" is the specifier. "You are like rain to creation in abundance of benefit." "May you never cease to be Rahman": he invoked its permanence, being merciful to them. Rahman is specific to God, so applying it to another is ignorance or obstinacy. It is said that what is specific to Him is the definite form with al.]]

This is a case of their obstinacy in their disbelief. If you say: How do you say "Allah is Rahman"; do you inflect it or not? [[Mahmud, may God the Exalted have mercy on him, said: "If you say, how do you say 'Allah is Rahman,' do you inflect it or not... etc.?" Ahmad said: I wonder, after the impossibility of fa'lana and fa'la, what determined analogizing it to 'atshan rather than nadman, when analogy to nadman is supported by the original principle in nouns, which is inflection? I say: What determined it is that the pattern of sakran and 'atshan is more common than the pattern of nadman, and when it may be from either, taking it by the more common is preferable. Also, rahman and 'atshan share the absence of a feminine in fa'lana, unlike nadman, so taking it by 'atshan is preferable. Then he said: Others have reported disagreement about inflecting rahman when it is undefined, and he based it on determining the cause for the prohibition of inflection of 'atshan: is it the existence of fa'la, so that rahman is inflected, or the absence of fa'lana, so that inflection is prohibited? This too is a deficient view. More complete than both is to say: 'atshan is by consensus not inflected, and the prohibition of its inflection is due to the resemblance of its two extra letters to the two feminine markers, and the resemblance revolves around the existence of fa'la and the absence of fa'lana. Either the two attributes of resemblance together are independently sufficient, or each one independently explains the resemblance, or one alone in turn: these are four possibilities. If the resemblance requires the combination or the existence of fa'la alone, rahman is inflected; if each of the two is independently sufficient, or the resemblance is by the absence of fa'lana alone, rahman is prevented from inflection. Then only the determination of what produced the resemblance in 'atshan between its two extra letters and the two feminine markers remains among the four possibilities, and on it inflection and non-inflection depend. The truth is that each of the two mentioned matters is independently sufficient to produce the resemblance, so rahman is not inflected because one of the two linked causes of resemblance exists, namely the absence of fa'lana on this assumption. We say this because the absence of fa'lana in it amounts to the impossibility of adding the feminine marker to its extra letters, as with the impossibility of adding them to the two feminine markers, so the resemblance arises in this respect. The existence of fa'la establishes that its masculine is restricted to one pattern and its feminine to another pattern, so it resembles af'al and fa'la in that each is restricted to a pattern other than the other; this is another aspect of resemblance. Whoever reflects on Sibawayh's words will understand what I have established. If it is said: the outcome of that is the suitability of each of the two mentioned matters to the production of resemblance, so what indicates that each one independently is a cause of resemblance? Why not let the combination be the cause, and then rahman would be inflected, being one of the four previous possibilities? I say: The prohibition of inflecting the proper name 'Imran indicates the independence of each of the two matters in producing the resemblance that prevents inflection, since 'Imran as a proper name has no fa'la, and it is by consensus not inflected. I say: Here may God have mercy on him slipped, and the skilled may slip, because the consideration of the existence of fa'la or the absence of fa'lana applies only to adjectives; in nouns, the condition is definiteness as a proper name, not the existence of fa'la or the absence of fa'lana.]] I say: I analogize it to its fellows of its pattern, namely such as 'atshan, ghartan, and sakran, so I do not inflect it.

If you say: a condition for the prohibition of inflecting fa'lan is that it be fa'lan with fa'la as its feminine, and its restriction to God precludes it being fa'lan with fa'la, so why do you prohibit inflection? I say: Just as that precludes it having a feminine in fa'la, like 'atsha, so it precludes it having a feminine in fa'lana, like nadmana. Thus no weight is given to the prohibition of the feminine because of the accidental restriction, and it is required to return to the original state before the restriction, which is analogy to its counterparts.

If you say: what is the meaning of describing God, exalted is He, with mercy, and that it means tenderness and compassion, and from it "womb" (rahim) because it bends over what is in it? I say: It is a metaphor for His bestowing favor on His servants, since when a king inclines toward his subjects and is moved with compassion for them, he bestows on them his kindness and favor, just as when harshness and severity overtake him, he treats them roughly and withholds from them his goodness and kindness. If you say: why did he put first what is more intense of the two attributes before what is less? [[Mahmud, may God the Exalted have mercy on him, said: "If you say, why did he put first what is more intense of the two attributes over what is less... etc.?" Ahmad, may God have mercy on him, said: The analogy was to place the lesser of the two attributes first, because placing the higher of them first and then following with the lesser involves a kind of repetition, since the attainment of the more intense necessarily entails the attainment of the lesser, so mentioning it afterward adds nothing. This is not so in the reverse, for it is an ascent from the lesser to an increase by the excellence of the higher, which did not precede anything that entails it. For this reason this order is specific to affirmation. As for negation, it is the reverse, in which the higher is placed first. You say: "So-and-so is not a scholar nor a mere (tahrir)"... and if you reversed it, you would fall into repetition, since negating the lesser from him necessarily entails negating the higher. All this derives from the generality of the lesser and the specificity of the more intense, and affirming the more specific entails affirming the more general, and negating the more general entails negating the more specific.]] The analogy would be ascent from the lesser to the higher, as in the saying: "So-and-so is a learned scholar, a brave warrior, and a generous, overflowing giver." I say: When He said al-Rahman, it encompassed the great and mighty blessings and their roots, and He followed it with al-Rahim as a complement and a supplement, to encompass what is fine and subtle among them.

Praise (al-hamd) and commendation (al-madh) are close in meaning. Both are laudation and extolling of what is beautiful, whether it be a blessing or something else. You say: "I praised the man for his favour," and "I praised him for his lineage and his bravery."

As for gratitude (al-shukr), it is specifically for a blessing (ni'mah). It is carried out by the heart, the tongue, and the limbs. The poet said:

*"Your favours from me have benefited you in three ways: my hand, my tongue, and my veiled conscience.*
*My thanks were never equal to your bounty, but I have striven to find a way in my utmost effort."*

Meaning: my honouring of you was not adequate to the right of your giving, but I sought, through striving to honour you, a way. He explained this by saying: your favour to me has benefited you through my hand, my tongue, and my heart, and their actions are for you. Al-Sayyid al-Sharif said: this is an indirect proof that shukr is applied to the actions of these three sources, and an explanation that he made them a recompense for the blessing. Whatever is a recompense for a blessing by custom is called shukr linguistically. It is as if he said: your favour to me has been great, so I am obliged to render every kind of gratitude to you, and he exaggerated in this until he made their sources (of action) the property of his benefactors. It has been said that al-ni'maa (the favours) is a plural of al-ni'mah, but the wording of "the hand" suggests that it has the same meaning. The narration of the first verse after the second is better in placement and clearer as evidence.

Praise by the tongue alone is one branch of gratitude. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Praise is the head of gratitude; Allah does not thank a servant who does not praise Him." (Narrated by ʿAbd al-Razzaq from Maʿmar from Qatadah from ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAmr, may Allah be pleased with them both, as a marfūʿ report. Its chain has a break. It is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbas similarly, transmitted by al-Baghawi in his tafsir of (Subhan), and in its chain is Nasr ibn Hammad, who is weak.)

He made it the head of gratitude because mentioning the blessing with the tongue and praising its giver is more widespread for it, and a better indication of its place than belief (i'tiqad) and the conduct of the limbs, because the work of the heart is hidden and the work of the limbs admits of uncertainty. This is unlike the work of the tongue, which is speech that makes clear every hidden thing and reveals every ambiguity.

The opposite of praise (al-hamd) is blame (al-dhamm), and the opposite of gratitude (al-shukr) is ingratitude (al-kufran). The nominative case of "al-hamd" is due to its being the subject of a nominal sentence (al-ibtida'), and its predicate is the adverbial phrase "lillah" (to Allah). Its original form is the accusative. [Mahmud, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "The original for al-hamd is the accusative..." etc. Ahmad said: Because the nominative is more firmly established, Sibawayh preferred, in the saying of one who says "I saw Zayd, and behold he has the knowledge of the jurists," the nominative; and in a saying like "I saw Zayd, and behold he has the voice of a donkey," the accusative. The secret of the difference between the nominative and the accusative is that the accusative implies an action, and the form of an action implies renewal and occurrence, whereas the nominative does not. It only calls for a noun, and that noun is a fixed attribute. Do you not see that what is implied with the accusative is "we praise Allah with praise," while with the nominative it is "praise is established for Allah or settled."]

The accusative form is the reading of some, with its verb suppressed, and it is one of the verbal nouns (al-masadir) which the Arabs put in the accusative with suppressed verbs, carrying the sense of informing, like their sayings "shukran" (thanks), "kufran" (ingratitude), "ʿajaban" (how strange!), and what resembles them. Among them are "subhanaka" (glory be to You) and "maʿadh Allah" (God forbid). They treat these as in the place of their verbs and let them stand in their place. For this reason they do not use them with the verb, and they regard their use with it as an abrogated law (al-shari'ah al-mansukhah). The shift from the accusative to the nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence serves to indicate the stability and permanence of the meaning. From this is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿They said, "Peace!" He said, "Peace."﴾ The second "peace" was put in the nominative to indicate that Abraham, peace be upon him, greeted them with a greeting better than theirs, because the nominative indicates the permanence of peace for them, not its renewal and occurrence. The meaning is: "We praise Allah with praise." For this reason it was said: ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾, because it is an explanation of their praise of Him, as if it were said: "How do you praise?" It was answered: "You alone we worship."

*Al-Rabb* means the owner. From it is the saying of Safwan to Abu Sufyan: "That a man of Quraysh should be my lord is dearer to me than that a man of Hawazin should be my lord." [This is a statement (mawquf) from a companion. Ibn Ishaq said in al-Maghazi: "Asim ibn Umar ibn Qatadah related to me from ʿAbd al-Rahman ibn Jabir ibn ʿAbdullah from his father, in the story of Hunayn," and in it is this saying of Safwan. Ibn Habban related it in his Sahih by this route, and al-Bayhaqi in al-Dala'il. Juwayriyyah narrated it from Malik from al-Zuhri as a mursal report. Al-Daraqutni related it in al-Gharib.
(Note) It appears in one report that Safwan said this to Abu Sufyan, while in al-Zuhri's mursal report he said it to his cousin (ibn akhihi), and in al-Maghazi he said it to his brother, the son of his mother, Kaladah. Abu Ya'la related it through the route of Ibn Ishaq.] You say: "rabbahu yarubbuhu, fa-huwa rabb," just as you say: "namma ʿalayhi yanummu, fa-huwa numm."

It is permissible that it is an attribute by way of the verbal noun for emphasis, just as "al-ʿadl" (justice) is used as an attribute. They did not apply the word "rabb" except to Allah alone. When used of others, it is restricted by an annexation (idafah), as in the sayings "rabb al-dar" (master of the house) and "rabb al-naqah" (owner of the she-camel), and in the Exalted's words: ﴿Return to your lord﴾ (12:50) and ﴿He is my lord; he has made my dwelling good﴾ (12:23). Zayd ibn ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with them both, read "rabba al-ʿalamin" with the accusative, as an expression of praise. It has also been said that it is governed by what is indicated by "al-hamdu lillah," as if it were said: "We praise Allah, Lord of the worlds."

*Al-ʿAlam* is the name for those who possess knowledge, from among the angels and the two weighty ones (humans and jinn). [Mahmud, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "Al-ʿalam is the name for those who possess knowledge from among the angels..." etc. Ahmad, may Allah have mercy on him, said: His explanation of the plural by its conveying comprehensiveness of every genus beneath it is open to question, for "ʿalam," as he established it, is a noun of genus defined by the genus-definite article, so that "ʿalam," which is singular, is more indicative of comprehensiveness than as a plural. Imam al-Haramayn, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "Al-tamr" (dates) is more fitting for the comprehensiveness of the genus than "al-tumur" (types of dates), because "al-tamr" flows over the genus without a verbal form, while "al-tumur" refers it to an imagined sense of totality. Then comprehensiveness follows with the plural form, and there is ambiguity in the plural form. End of his words. The verification of this, and of everything that is pluralised among nouns of genus and then defined by the genus-definite article, is that it conveys two matters: one, that this genus contains different kinds; the other, that it comprehensively includes all of its kinds. But what conveys the difference of kinds is the plural, and what conveys the comprehensiveness of all of them is the definite article. Do you not see that when it is plural without the definite article it indicates difference of kinds, and then when it is defined it conveys comprehensiveness not dependent on plurality, since this is the rule of its singular when defined? So al-Zamakhshari's statement, "the benefit of pluralising 'al-ʿalamin' is comprehensiveness," is rejected, since this benefit is established even without the plural. Imam al-Haramayn's statement, "the plural supports the indication of comprehensiveness, due to what we imagine of being referred to totality," is rejected, because the benefit of the plural is to indicate difference of kinds, and difference does not contradict their comprehensiveness by the singular form confirmed by the genus-definite article. If he means that the plural conjures an indication to kinds known to be its place, then this imagination is better expressed by the singular. Therefore "ʿalam" is plural to convey the difference of kinds beneath it of jinn, humans, and angels, and it is defined to convey the universality of Allah's lordship over all its kinds. The clarification of this exposition: if we supposed a genus with nothing beneath it but equal individuals, which is what non-grammarians call the lowest species, this could not be pluralised in any way, neither defined nor indefinite. By this benefit, the statement of Imam al-Haramayn, "'al-tumur' is plural in form," is rebutted, since there is no meaning in pluralising a plural as in "nawq/niyaq" and "aniq." As for al-Zamakhshari's explanation of its being pluralised with the sound masculine plural suffix (wa-w-n) by its indication of the attribute of knowledge, so that it is attached to the attributes of rational beings, this is correct if the matter is based on it applying only to the possessors of knowledge. But on the view that it is a name for everything existing other than Allah, further consideration is needed as to giving precedence to the rational in the plural over the non-rational.]

It has also been said: "Everything by which the Creator is known, of bodies and accidents." If you say: why is it pluralised? I say: so that it includes every genus that is named by it. If you say: it is a noun, not an attribute, and the sound masculine plural with waw and nun is used only for attributes of rational beings, or what is in their category, such as proper names?

I say: this is permitted because of the attributive meaning in it, which is the indication of the meaning of knowledge.

Praise (al-hamd) and commendation (al-madh) are close in meaning. Both are laudation and extolling of what is beautiful, whether it be a blessing or something else. You say: "I praised the man for his favour," and "I praised him for his lineage and his bravery."

As for gratitude (al-shukr), it is specifically for a blessing (ni'mah). It is carried out by the heart, the tongue, and the limbs. The poet said:

*"Your favours from me have benefited you in three ways: my hand, my tongue, and my veiled conscience.*
*My thanks were never equal to your bounty, but I have striven to find a way in my utmost effort."*

Meaning: my honouring of you was not adequate to the right of your giving, but I sought, through striving to honour you, a way. He explained this by saying: your favour to me has benefited you through my hand, my tongue, and my heart, and their actions are for you. Al-Sayyid al-Sharif said: this is an indirect proof that shukr is applied to the actions of these three sources, and an explanation that he made them a recompense for the blessing. Whatever is a recompense for a blessing by custom is called shukr linguistically. It is as if he said: your favour to me has been great, so I am obliged to render every kind of gratitude to you, and he exaggerated in this until he made their sources (of action) the property of his benefactors. It has been said that al-ni'maa (the favours) is a plural of al-ni'mah, but the wording of "the hand" suggests that it has the same meaning. The narration of the first verse after the second is better in placement and clearer as evidence.

Praise by the tongue alone is one branch of gratitude. From this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "Praise is the head of gratitude; Allah does not thank a servant who does not praise Him." (Narrated by ʿAbd al-Razzaq from Maʿmar from Qatadah from ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAmr, may Allah be pleased with them both, as a marfūʿ report. Its chain has a break. It is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbas similarly, transmitted by al-Baghawi in his tafsir of (Subhan), and in its chain is Nasr ibn Hammad, who is weak.)

He made it the head of gratitude because mentioning the blessing with the tongue and praising its giver is more widespread for it, and a better indication of its place than belief (i'tiqad) and the conduct of the limbs, because the work of the heart is hidden and the work of the limbs admits of uncertainty. This is unlike the work of the tongue, which is speech that makes clear every hidden thing and reveals every ambiguity.

The opposite of praise (al-hamd) is blame (al-dhamm), and the opposite of gratitude (al-shukr) is ingratitude (al-kufran). The nominative case of "al-hamd" is due to its being the subject of a nominal sentence (al-ibtida'), and its predicate is the adverbial phrase "lillah" (to Allah). Its original form is the accusative. [Mahmud, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "The original for al-hamd is the accusative..." etc. Ahmad said: Because the nominative is more firmly established, Sibawayh preferred, in the saying of one who says "I saw Zayd, and behold he has the knowledge of the jurists," the nominative; and in a saying like "I saw Zayd, and behold he has the voice of a donkey," the accusative. The secret of the difference between the nominative and the accusative is that the accusative implies an action, and the form of an action implies renewal and occurrence, whereas the nominative does not. It only calls for a noun, and that noun is a fixed attribute. Do you not see that what is implied with the accusative is "we praise Allah with praise," while with the nominative it is "praise is established for Allah or settled."]

The accusative form is the reading of some, with its verb suppressed, and it is one of the verbal nouns (al-masadir) which the Arabs put in the accusative with suppressed verbs, carrying the sense of informing, like their sayings "shukran" (thanks), "kufran" (ingratitude), "ʿajaban" (how strange!), and what resembles them. Among them are "subhanaka" (glory be to You) and "maʿadh Allah" (God forbid). They treat these as in the place of their verbs and let them stand in their place. For this reason they do not use them with the verb, and they regard their use with it as an abrogated law (al-shari'ah al-mansukhah). The shift from the accusative to the nominative as the subject of a nominal sentence serves to indicate the stability and permanence of the meaning. From this is the saying of the Exalted: ﴿They said, "Peace!" He said, "Peace."﴾ The second "peace" was put in the nominative to indicate that Abraham, peace be upon him, greeted them with a greeting better than theirs, because the nominative indicates the permanence of peace for them, not its renewal and occurrence. The meaning is: "We praise Allah with praise." For this reason it was said: ﴿You alone we worship, and You alone we ask for help﴾, because it is an explanation of their praise of Him, as if it were said: "How do you praise?" It was answered: "You alone we worship."

Recited: "Malik yawm al-din" (Master of the Day of Judgment), "Maalik," and "Malk" with the lam lightened. Abu Hanifa, may Allah be pleased with him, recited it in a way that indicates the restriction of praise to Him, and that He is truly deserving of it in His saying "All praise is for Allah" — this is evidence that whoever has these attributes, no one is more deserving than him of praise and commendation befitting him.

(إيا) is a detached pronoun in the accusative case. The suffixes attached to it, the kaf, the ha' and the ya' in your saying "iyyaka", "iyyahu" and "iyyaya", indicate second, third and first person respectively. They have no place in i'rab (grammatical case analysis), just as the kaf in "ara'aytaka" has no place. They are not pronouns in their own right. This is the view of al-Akhfash, and the scholars who verify matters hold it. As for what al-Khalil related from some Arabs, "When a man reaches sixty, then iyyahu and iyya al-shawwab", it is an anomalous usage that is not to be relied upon. The object is placed first to restrict the meaning, as in His saying ﴿Say: "Do you order me to worship other than Allah?"﴾ and ﴿Say: "Shall I seek a lord other than Allah?"﴾. The meaning is: "We single You out for worship, and single You out for seeking help."

It is also read as "iyyaka" with the ya' lightened, as "ayyaka" with the hamza opened and the ya' doubled, and as "hayyaka" with the hamza changed into ha'. Tufayl al-Ghanawi said:

"So hayyaka and the matter which, if its watering-places spread wide, its outlets become narrow for you."

[The verse is attributed to Mudrris ibn Rub'i, and some say to Tufayl. Hayyaka is originally iyyaka, its hamza changed to ha'. It is in the accusative by a necessarily omitted verb, and "al-amr" (the matter) is conjoined to it. The original sense is: "Beware of meeting yourself and the matter", and everything apart from the pronoun of address and what is conjoined to it has been omitted because of frequent usage, and because the context of warning calls for haste and brevity. It is also said that the original was: "Keep yourself away from the matter and keep the matter away from yourself", and so it was omitted for this reason. The causes of entering into the matter are likened to watering-places, that is, the places where one arrives at water, and the causes of leaving it are likened to outlets, that is, the places of return. Each of these is an explicit metaphor (isti'ara tasrihiyya). As for likening the matter to something that has watering-places and outlets, like water, in the manner of the implicit metaphor (al-makniyya), that falls outside the rules of rhetorical clarity, because "the matter" applies to everything; so restricting it to something other than water and then likening it to water is intentional, not inherent in the word. It is also transmitted thus:

"So iyyaka and the matter which, if its watering-places spread wide, the outlets become narrow for you.

So it is not good for a man to excuse himself, and he has no excuser from among all people."

That is, a man's excusing himself is not good, meaning, his acceptance of his own excuse after he has fallen into the predicament. His saying "and he has no excuser" is a circumstantial clause (jumla haliyya), and on this reading the rhyme-letter should be ra'.]

Worship (al-'ibada) is the utmost extent of submission and humility. From it comes the phrase "a garment with 'ibda", meaning one that is at the extreme of thickness and strength of weave. For this reason the word is used only for submission to Allah, the Exalted, because He is the bestower of the greatest blessings, so He is deserving of the utmost degree of submission.

If you ask: why has the expression shifted from the third person to the second person? I answer: this is called iltifat (shift of grammatical person) in the science of eloquence ('ilm al-bayan). It may occur from third person to second, from second to third, and from third to first, as in His saying ﴿until when you were in the ship and they were running with them﴾, and His saying ﴿And Allah is He who sends the winds, so they raise clouds, and We drive them﴾. Imru' al-Qays made three shifts in three verses:

"Your night has stretched out with al-Ithmid, and the friend has slept, while you have not slept.

It spent the night, and the night was for it like the night of the one with the bleary, aching eye.

That is news that came to me, and I was informed of it concerning Abu al-Aswad."

[This is by Imru' al-Qays ibn Hujr the pre-Islamic poet, though Ibn Hisham said it was an error, and that its speaker is Imru' al-Qays ibn 'Abis, a Companion; it is also said to be said of 'Amr ibn Ma'dikarib. Al-Ithmid, like Ahmad, may have its mim vowelled, and it may be read with a kasra: it is the name of a place. Al-'a'ir is a solid noun applied to a speck that makes the eye weep, to inflammation of the eye, and to anything that ails the eye. In the poem there are three shifts, but the first is so only according to al-Sakkaki alone: namely, that the expected form was to speak in the first person, but he shifted to address, and that is in the first verse. The second is his turning from address to the third person in the second verse. The third is his turning from the third person to the first in the third verse. The majority treat the first as an instance of tajrid (abstraction, where a speaker addresses himself as if another). "Abu al-Aswad" is the kunya of the man whom the poet is lamenting; it is also said that the informer was named Zalim ibn 'Amr, and he was the paternal uncle of Imru' al-Qays. It is also said that "abi" is annexed to the first-person ya', and "al-Aswad" is its epithet. It is also transmitted as: "concerning the Banu al-Aswad".]

This is in accordance with their custom of varying their speech and handling it in different ways. Also, when speech is transferred from one style to another, it refreshes the listener's energy and rouses him to attend, rather than keeping it in a single style. Its positions may also be singled out for particular benefits. What is specific to this place is this: when He mentioned the One deserving of praise and attributed to Him those great qualities, knowledge became attached to a known object of great importance, deserving of praise, of the utmost submission, and of seeking help in grave matters. So that object, distinguished by those qualities, was addressed, and it was said: "Iyyaka, O You whose attributes these are; we single You out for worship and for seeking help. We do not worship other than You, nor do we seek help from other than You." This makes the address more evident that worship belongs to Him, because of that distinction which makes worship due to none but Him.

If you ask: why is seeking help joined with worship? I answer: so that what the servants draw near to their Lord by, and what they seek from Him and need from Him, may be combined.

If you ask: why is worship placed before seeking help? I answer: because presenting the means before asking for the need is so that they may deserve to be answered. [Al-Zamakhshari, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "If you ask why worship is placed before seeking help..." Ahmad said: The creed of the People of the Sunna is that the servant does not make his Lord owe him a reward, exalted is Allah above that. Reward, according to us, whether help in worldly worship or the various forms of bliss in the Hereafter, is not obligatory upon Allah, the Exalted, but is rather a grace and kindness from Him. In a hadith, the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "None of you will enter Paradise by his deeds." It was said: "Not even you, Messenger of Allah?" He said: "Not even me, unless Allah covers me with His mercy." Moreover, reason rules out that anything could be obligatory upon Allah, the Exalted. Reason and revelation both establish that nothing is obligatory upon Him, the Exalted; and both establish that His report is true and His promise is sound, meaning that it is necessarily true by reason that it will come to pass. So either al-Zamakhshari was lax in using the word "owed", and meant the necessity of the truth of the report, or he was following the principles of the innovators in holding that goodness is obligatory upon Allah, the Exalted, even without a promise.]

If you ask: why is seeking help stated without a specified object? I answer: so that it covers every matter in which help is sought. The best reading is that seeking help is intended both from Him and by His granting success in performing worship, and His saying "Guide us" ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ clarifies what is sought of help, as if it were said: "How shall I help you?" and they said: "Guide us to the straight path." This is better because it harmonises the speech and each part holds the other. Ibn Habish read "nasta'in", with a kasra on the nun.

Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on surah 1, verse 6:

Hadá (هدى, "to guide") originally takes its object with the preposition lām or with ilā, as in the words of God Most High: ﴿Indeed, this Qur'an guides to that which is most upright﴾ [17:9], and ﴿And indeed, you guide to a straight path﴾ [42:52]. It is therefore treated in the manner of ikhtār (اختار, "to choose") in the words of God Most High: ﴿And Moses chose from his people﴾ [7:155].

The meaning of asking for guidance, while they are already guided, is asking for an increase of guidance through the granting of divine favour (luṭf), as in the words of God Most High: ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance﴾ [47:17], and ﴿And those who strive in Us, We will surely guide them to Our paths﴾ [29:69]. It is reported from ʿAlī and Ubayy, may God be pleased with them both, that they read: "Make us firm (thabbitnā) [in guidance]." The form of the imperative and the form of the supplication are one, because each of them is a request, and they differ only in rank.

ʿAbdullāh read: "Guide us" as arshidnā (أرشدنا).

(Al-ṣirāṭ) is the main road (al-jādda), from saraṭa al-shayʾ (سرط الشيء), meaning "he swallowed it," because it swallows up the travellers when they take it, just as it is called luqam (لقم), because it engulfs (yalqimuhum) them. The word ṣirāṭ comes from changing the sīn into a ṣād because of the ṭāʾ, as in his saying: muṣayṭir in place of musaytir (مسيطر). The ṣād may be pronounced with the sound of the zāy, and it has been read in all of these ways. The most eloquent of these is the pure ṣād, and this is the dialect of Quraysh, and it is the one preserved in the Imam (the standard codex). Its plural is ṣurūṭ (سرطا), like kitāb and kutub, and it is used as both masculine and feminine, like al-ṭarīq (the road) and al-sabīl (the way). What is meant is the path of truth, which is the religion of Islam.

**Commentary of al-Zamakhshari (al-Kashshaf) on Surah 1, verse 7:**

﴿The path of those upon whom You have bestowed favor﴾ is a substitute (badal, an apposition that replaces the preceding noun) for ﴿the straight path﴾. It has the force of repeating the governing verb, as if it had been said: (﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾), "Guide us to the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favor," just as He said: ﴿those who were oppressed﴾, meaning those among them who believed. If you ask: what is the purpose of the substitution, and why was it not said, "Guide us to the path of those upon whom You have bestowed favor"? I answer:

Its purpose is emphasis, because of the repetition and reiteration it contains, and the indication that the straight path is clarified and explained as "the path of the Muslims," so that this serves as a testimony to the path of the Muslims being straight in the most eloquent and emphatic way. This is like when you say: "Shall I direct you to the most generous and most virtuous of people? So-and-so." This is more eloquent in describing him with generosity and virtue than your saying: "Shall I direct you to So-and-so, the most generous and most virtuous?" Because you mentioned his name first in a general way, then in a detailed way, and you placed "So-and-so" as an explanation and clarification of "the most generous and most virtuous," thereby making him the standard of generosity and virtue. It is as if you said: "Whoever wants a man who combines the two qualities, let him go to So-and-so," for he is the specific, identified person in whom both are combined, without rival or contender.

﴿Those upon whom You have bestowed favor﴾ are the believers. The bestowal (inʿām) is stated without restriction so that it includes every kind of favor, [[Mahmud (al-Zamakhshari), may Allah have mercy on him, said: "And the bestowal is stated without restriction so that it includes every kind of bestowal." Ahmad (Ibn al-Munayyir), may Allah have mercy on him, said: The unrestricted statement of the bestowal indicates comprehensiveness, as in his saying: "The unrestricted statement of seeking help (istiʿana) encompasses every case in which help is sought." This is not accepted, for a verb does not have generality in its verbal noun. The truth is that the unrestricted statement only implies vagueness and generality, and the soul is more eager for the vague than for the specified, because hope attaches to every favor that comes to mind when it is indeterminate.]] because whoever has been favored with the blessing of Islam, no favor remains that has not reached him and encompassed him.

It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: they are the companions of Musa before they changed. It was also said: they are the prophets.

Ibn Masʿud recited: ﴿the path of those whom You have favored﴾. ﴿Not of those who have incurred wrath﴾ is a substitute for ﴿those upon whom You have bestowed favor﴾, meaning that those favored are those who were safe from the wrath of Allah and from misguidance. Or it is a qualifier (ṣifa, an adjective), meaning that they combined the unrestricted favor, which is the favor of faith, with safety from the wrath of Allah and from misguidance. If you ask: how can "ghayr" (other than, not) be a qualifier of a definite noun, when it does not become definite even if it is annexed to definites? I answer: ﴿those upon whom You have bestowed favor﴾ has no specification in it, as in the poet's saying:

*"And I pass by the base man who abuses me,*
*so I go on, and I say: 'It does not concern me.'*
*He is angry, filled with wrath to his very skin,*
*'Indeed, by your Lord, his anger pleases me.'"*

This is by a man from the Banu Salul. The phrase "who abuses me" is a qualifier of "the base man," even though it is preceded by the definite article, because the intended meaning is not a specific base man, as the context of praise shows. The article there is the mental (ʿahd dhihnī) article, not the external one, and what follows it is in meaning like an indefinite noun, so it is permissible to qualify it with a clause, even though a clause qualifies only an indefinite noun. This indicates that he is continually characterized by abuse, not only at the moment of passing, and this is what is meant. The apparent expectation was that he would say "then I passed on, then I say," but he used the past tense to indicate that this actually occurred from him. It is also narrated as: "then I forgive," meaning I refrain from him and from repaying him. It is possible that he intended the past tense to be replaced by the present tense to narrate the situation. The apparent view is that the clause is circumstantial: "I pass by the base man while he abuses me and I hear it, so I turn away from him and say that he does not aim at me with that abuse which I heard from him." The intention is not to describe him as continually abusive, since that does not appear with the restriction of the abuse to falling upon the pronoun of the passer-by. Moreover, it is possible to make the circumstantial clause a fixed state, which then indicates permanence. "He is angry, his skin filled with anger at me, but I do not care about that, for by the truth of your Lord, his anger pleases me. Let him persist in it and increase it." The word "ihab" means the skin before tanning, and even before flaying, as it is here.

It is also because "those who have incurred wrath" and "those who are astray" are the opposite of "those upon whom You have bestowed favor." So in "ghayr" there is an indeterminacy that prevents it from becoming definite.

It is recited in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl). This is the reading of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and of ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab, and it is also transmitted from Ibn Kathir. The circumstantial referent (dhu al-ḥāl) is the pronoun in ﴿upon them﴾, and the governing verb is ﴿You have bestowed favor﴾.

It was said: ﴿those who have incurred wrath﴾ are the Jews, based on the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿whom Allah has cursed and upon whom He is wrathful﴾. And ﴿those who are astray﴾ are the Christians, based on the saying of the Exalted: ﴿They have already gone astray before and led many astray﴾.

If you ask: what is the meaning of the wrath of Allah? I answer: it is the intention to take vengeance [[Mahmud, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "The meaning of wrath from Allah, exalted is He, is the intention to take vengeance…" etc. Ahmad said: He included in this what, in his view, necessitates the obligation of threatening the disobedient, which is not the doctrine of the People of the Sunnah. Rather, for them the matter concerning the believer who disobeys is left to Allah's will. Among them, Allah may intend to punish him and take vengeance upon him, and that will certainly happen; and among them, Allah may intend to pardon him and reward him out of His grace. Moreover, "those who have incurred wrath" and "those who are astray" refer to disbelievers, and their threat certainly occurs and is intended. And Allah is the Granter of success. I say: al-Zamakhshari, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "The wrath from Allah is the intention to take vengeance upon the disobedient, etc.," which does not indicate what he explained. For the obligation of threatening the disobedient is not known from it.

The wrath from Allah, according to the People of the Sunnah and the Mu'tazila, is an expression of what al-Zamakhshari, may Allah have mercy on him, mentioned, except that according to the People of the Sunnah, Allah, if He wills, punishes the one who commits a major sin, and if He wills, forgives him. According to the Mu'tazila, his punishment is obligatory. So according to the Mu'tazila it is clear that wrath is an expression of the intention to take vengeance. According to the People of the Sunnah: if He forgives him, there is no wrath; and if He does not forgive him, then His wrath is an expression of what was mentioned.]] against the disobedient, and the infliction of punishment upon them, and that He does to them what a king does when he is angry with one under his authority. We seek refuge in Allah from His wrath and ask Him for His good pleasure and His mercy.

If you ask: what is the difference between the first ﴿upon them﴾ and the second ﴿upon them﴾? I answer: the first has the place of accusative as object, and the second has the place of nominative as subject.

If you ask: why was ﴿lā﴾ (not) inserted into ﴿wa lā al-ḍāllīn﴾? I answer: because "ghayr" contains the meaning of negation, as if it had been said: "neither those who have incurred wrath nor those who are astray." You may say: "I, Zayd, am not striking," while it is impermissible to say: "I, Zayd, am like one striking," because it is equivalent to saying: "I, Zayd, am not a striker."

It is reported from ʿUmar and ʿAli, may Allah be pleased with them both, that they both recited: ﴿and ghayr al-ḍāllīn﴾. Ayyub al-Sakhtiyani recited: ﴿wa lā al-ḍallīn﴾ with a hamza, as ʿAmr ibn ʿUbayd recited: ﴿wa lā jann﴾. This is a dialect of those who strive to escape the meeting of two unvocalized letters. Among them is what Abu Zayd reported from their saying: "shāʾbah" and "daʾbah."

**Amin**: a sound that is used as the name of the verb "istajib" (answer), just as "ruwayd," "ḥayhal," and "halumma" are sounds used as the names of the verbs "amhil" (wait), "asriʿ" (hurry), and "aqbil" (come). It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the meaning of "amin," and he said: "Do it." It has two dialects: lengthening its alif and shortening it. The poet said:

*"And may Allah have mercy on a servant who says 'Amin'."*

[[*"O Lord, You are the Possessor of kindness and forgiveness,*
*who spend the night in well-being, the nights of lovers,*
*those who remember passion after they have slept,*
*those who fall upon their hands, prostrate,*
*O Lord, do not strip me of her love ever,*
*and may Allah have mercy on a servant who says 'Amin'."*

By Qays ibn Muʿadh al-Mulawwah, the madman of Layla al-ʿAmiriyya. His longing for her intensified, so his father took him to the Kaʿba to ask Allah that He might cure him, and he took hold of the ring of its door and said that. The supplication "for the nights of lovers" is a rational metonymy (majaz ʿaqlī); in reality it is for them. He made clear that their sleep is not the usual kind, by his saying: "those who fall upon their hands," "prostrate upon their faces" in bewilderment and intoxication. Then he prayed that Allah perpetuate her love, and he prayed for whoever says "Amin" after his supplication. "Amin" is a verb-name, meaning "answer, O Allah, this supplication." It is with the lengthened alif, and it is permissible to shorten it.]]

And he said:

*"Fatḥal has withdrawn from me when I called him,*
*'Amin,' so Allah increased the distance between us."*

By Jubayr, who had asked Fatḥal al-Asadi, but he turned away from him, so he invoked against him. It is narrated as "Fatḥal withdrew from me and from my father." "Amin" is with a short hamza in the original Arabic dialect. As for the lengthened form, it is said to be non-Arabic, because "fāʿīl" does not occur in the language of the Arabs. It was also said: its origin is the short form, and its hamza was lengthened; it is a verb-name meaning "answer," and its position is after what follows it. It is placed first out of eagerness for the request to be answered and for the supplication to be granted at the first instant. The fāʾ is causal with respect to what precedes it, meaning: "since he withdrew from me, increase, O Allah, the distance between us." "Baʿdan" (distance) may be a specification (tamyīz) or an object of a verb that is understood.]]

It is reported from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Gabriel, peace be upon him, taught me to say 'Amin' when I finished reciting the Opening of the Book." [[I have not found it in this form. In the book of supplications by Ibn Abi Shayba, from the narration of Abu Maysara, one of the senior Successors, he said: "Gabriel, peace be upon him, recited the Opening of the Book to the Prophet (ﷺ), and when he said 'nor of those who are astray,' he said to him: Say 'Amin.' And he said 'Amin.'" I say: and in Abu Dawud from Abu Zuhayr, he said: "Amin is like the seal upon the document." And Ibn Mardawayh reported from Abu Hurayra, traced to the Prophet: "Amin is the seal of the Lord of the worlds upon His believing servants," and it is in the supplications of al-Tabarani.]] and he said: "It is like a seal upon a document." It is not part of the Qur'an, as evidence that it is not recorded in the copies of the Qur'an.

It is reported from al-Hasan: the imam should not say it, because he is the one who supplicates. The same is reported from Abu Hanifa, may Allah have mercy on him. The well-known position of him and his companions is that one says it quietly. Silent recitation of it was narrated by ʿAbd Allah ibn Mughaffal and Anas from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). [[I have not found it from either of them.]] According to al-Shafiʿi, one says it aloud. It is reported from Wa'il ibn Hujr that the Prophet (ﷺ) used to say "Amin" when he recited "nor of those who are astray," and he raised his voice with it.
